title: Administrative Tribunal Bangladesh: Government Service Lawsuits, Dismissal & Pension Guide
metaTitle: Administrative Tribunal Bangladesh: Government Service Cases
metaDescription: Facing unlawful dismissal or pension withholding in Bangladesh? How to file cases before the Administrative Tribunal under Act No. VII of 1981.
keywords: government servant discipline and appeal rules
heroIntro: For civil servants, government officers, public school educators, and employees of autonomous statutory corporations in Bangladesh, public service is governed by specialized constitutional and statutory protections. When a government employee is subjected to wrongful dismissal, compulsory retirement, punitive demotion, arbitrary transfer, supersession in promotion, or withholding of pension and gratuity benefits, ordinary civil courts lack jurisdiction. Under Article 117 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981), exclusive judicial jurisdiction to adjudicate terms and conditions of public service resides with the Administrative Tribunal and the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. This comprehensive legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and administrative litigation specialist in Dhaka, details the statutory framework, departmental appeal prerequisites, limitation deadlines, and litigation strategies before the Administrative Tribunals and Supreme Court.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Overview: How to File a Case in the Administrative Tribunal
quickAnswer.heading: Quick Overview: How to File a Case in the Administrative Tribunal
quickAnswer.text: Under the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981), public servants must satisfy strict procedural prerequisites before invoking the Tribunal's jurisdiction. First, the employee must exhaust all internal departmental remedies by filing a Departmental Appeal or Review before the higher administrative authority under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 2018. If the departmental appeal is rejected, or if no decision is rendered within two (2) months of filing, the employee must file an Administrative Tribunal Case within six (6) months under Section 4(2). The Administrative Tribunal possesses powers to quash punitive departmental orders, order reinstatement with full back pay, rectify seniorities, and release withheld pension funds. Decisions of the Tribunal can be challenged before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Dhaka, followed by a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court.

Exclusive Jurisdiction: Governs terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic and statutory public authorities.
Departmental Appeal Prerequisite: Mandatory exhaustion of internal departmental appeals before filing before the Tribunal.
Statutory Limitation (Section 4): Case must be instituted within six (6) months from the date of the departmental appeal decision, or after two months of silence.
Appellate Hierarchy: Administrative Tribunal → Administrative Appellate Tribunal (Dhaka) → Appellate Division of Supreme Court (Article 103).
Permissible Remedies: Quashing termination, setting aside compulsory retirement, ordering promotion retroactively, and releasing pension/gratuity.
Bar on Civil Courts: Ordinary Assistant Judge or Subordinate Civil Courts have zero jurisdiction over public service disputes.

sections.title: 1. Constitutional Mandate: Article 117 & Act No. VII of 1981
sections.content:
In the legal structure of Bangladesh, public employment is treated not as a private master-servant contract, but as a public status safeguarded by the Constitution. Under Article 117(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, Parliament is empowered to establish Administrative Tribunals to exercise exclusive jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic.

To implement this constitutional guarantee, Parliament enacted the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981). Section 4 of the Act vests exclusive original jurisdiction in Administrative Tribunals to hear and determine applications made by public servants regarding their service conditions, disciplinary punishments, pensions, and statutory rights. Under Article 117(2), once an Administrative Tribunal is established for a matter, no other court—including the High Court Division under Article 102 writ jurisdiction—can entertain proceedings regarding that matter, subject to very narrow exceptions concerning vires of statutes or patent absence of jurisdiction.

This makes the Administrative Tribunal the indispensable judicial battleground for any civil servant seeking redress against arbitrary government action. The presiding member of the Tribunal is a senior judicial officer (typically of the rank of District Judge), ensuring impartial judicial scrutiny over executive excesses.

sections.title: 2. Jurisdiction: Who Can File Before the Administrative Tribunal?
sections.content:
Understanding which categories of employees fall within the protective umbrella of the Administrative Tribunal is vital before filing an application:

  • Persons in the Service of the Republic: All members of the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) cadres, administrative officers, ministry officials, magistracy staff, police personnel, and non-cadre government employees holding posts in government directorates and departments.
  • Statutory Public Authorities: Employees of statutory bodies, corporations, and state institutions established by act of Parliament (such as Bangladesh Power Development Board, WASA, RAJUK, and nationalized banks) where the relevant service rules notify tribunal jurisdiction.
  • Retired Civil Servants & Pensioners: Former public servants whose post-retirement pension, gratuity, general provident fund (GPF), or medical allowances are unlawfully withheld or delayed.
  • Excluded Categories: Members of the Defense Forces (Army, Navy, Air Force) governed by their respective military acts, and staff of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, who are excluded under Section 3 of the Act.

sections.title: 3. The Mandatory Departmental Appeal Prerequisite
sections.content:
A critical procedural trap that causes many administrative service lawsuits to be dismissed at the threshold is failure to exhaust internal administrative remedies. Under Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980, the Tribunal is statutorily barred from entertaining an application unless the applicant has first exhausted all departmental appeals, representations, or reviews available under applicable service rules.

Under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 2018:

  1. When a punishing authority passes an adverse disciplinary order (such as dismissal, removal, reduction in rank, or stoppage of increment), the employee must submit a formal Departmental Appeal within thirty (30) days to the designated appellate authority (e.g. Secretary of the Ministry or Director General).
  2. The departmental appeal must clearly state the procedural irregularities of the inquiry, violation of natural justice, and substantive defenses.
  3. If the appellate authority rejects the appeal, the prerequisite is met.
  4. The Two-Month Rule: If the appellate authority fails to render a decision within two (2) months from the date of filing the departmental appeal, Section 4(2) allows the employee to treat the appeal as constructively exhausted and approach the Administrative Tribunal directly.

sections.title: 4. Strict Limitation Windows Under Section 4 of the Act
sections.content:
Facing a government service dispute, dismissal or pension withholding? Contact our administrative law chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. We represent public servants across all ministries.

Limitation in public service litigation is strictly enforced. The Administrative Tribunals Act 1980 does not allow for indefinite delays, and Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1908 cannot be casually invoked to condone gross negligence.

The statutory limitation rules under Section 4(2) dictate that an application must be filed before the Administrative Tribunal within:

  • Six (6) Months from Appeal Decision: If the departmental appellate authority delivers a formal written order rejecting or modifying the appeal, the case must be filed within precisely six months from the date of communication of that order.
  • Six Months Following the Two-Month Silence Window: If the departmental authority sits on the appeal without passing an order, the case must be filed within six months immediately following the expiry of the initial two-month waiting period (i.e. between month 2 and month 8 from the appeal filing date).

Filing even one day after the statutory limitation deadline results in threshold dismissal of the application. An advocate must verify postal tracking receipts and service delivery memos before drafting the petition.

sections.title: 6. Grounds for Challenging Departmental Inquiries & Penalties
sections.content:
When challenging disciplinary punishments—such as dismissal, removal from service, compulsory retirement, or reduction in pay scale—the Administrative Tribunal scrutinizes whether the administrative inquiry complied with natural justice and statutory rules.

Established grounds for quashing disciplinary orders include:

  • Denial of Natural Justice: The employee was denied an adequate opportunity to submit a written statement of defense, examine prosecution documents, or cross-examine witnesses who testified against them.
  • Biased Inquiry Officer: The departmental inquiry officer was a subordinate of the complainant or demonstrated open prejudice during the inquiry proceedings.
  • Failure to Supply Inquiry Report: The punishing authority failed to serve a copy of the inquiry officer's report along with a second show-cause notice prior to imposing the final penalty, depriving the employee of the right to rebut adverse findings.
  • Disproportionate Penalty: Imposing capital administrative punishment (dismissal or removal) for minor administrative oversights violates the established doctrine of proportionality recognized by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

sections.title: 7. Remedies for Withheld Pension, Gratuity & Retirement Benefits
sections.content:
One of the most frequent grievances presented by senior public servants and their families involves the arbitrary withholding of post-retirement pension, gratuity, and leave encashment benefits. Decades of Supreme Court precedent, including landmark decisions of the Appellate Division, affirm that pension is not a bounty or charitable grace; it is property earned through long, honorable service protected under Article 42 of the Constitution.

Key principles enforced by the Administrative Tribunal include:

  1. No Withholding Without Judicial Conviction: Government departments cannot freeze or withhold pension or gratuity benefits based on preliminary audit objections, administrative inquiries, or unadjudicated departmental allegations that were never concluded during the officer's active service.
  2. Post-Retirement Disciplinary Inquiries Barred: Under the Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974, once an officer has formally retired and crossed the statutory retirement age, new departmental disciplinary proceedings cannot be instituted without explicit statutory authorization.
  3. Release of Family Pension: In the event of a public servant's death, surviving spouses and minor dependents can approach the Tribunal to secure immediate release of family pension and welfare benefits unlawfully held up by the Controller General of Accounts (CGA).

sections.title: 8. Appeals to Administrative Appellate Tribunal & Supreme Court
sections.content:
The decisions of the Administrative Tribunal are subject to a structured statutory appellate hierarchy centered in Dhaka:

  • The Administrative Appellate Tribunal (AAT): Established under Section 5 of the Act and sitting in Dhaka, the AAT comprises a Chairman (who is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court or is qualified to be such) and two member colleagues. An aggrieved public servant or the Government can file an appeal before the AAT within three (3) months from the date of the Administrative Tribunal's judgment under Section 6. The AAT has powers to confirm, modify, or reverse the tribunal's order.
  • Appellate Division of the Supreme Court (CPLA): Under Section 6A of the Act and Article 103 of the Constitution, no appeal lies from the AAT to the High Court Division. The sole avenue of further challenge is filing a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) directly before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh within thirty (30) days.
  • Execution of Decrees: Under Section 10A, the orders of the Administrative Tribunal and AAT are enforceable throughout Bangladesh as decrees of a civil court, compelling recalcitrant ministries to execute reinstatements and disburse funds.

sections.title: 9. Illustrative Scenario: Overturning Wrongful Compulsory Retirement
sections.content:
Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): A senior deputy secretary serving in a government ministry in Dhaka was abruptly served with a compulsory retirement order under Section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 after 26 years of distinguished service. The order cited 'public interest' but was triggered by the officer's refusal to approve an irregular public procurement tender favored by politically influential contractors. No formal charge sheet or inquiry had ever been conducted.

Faced with loss of dignity and severe pension reductions, the officer retained Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our legal team executed a structured administrative challenge:

  1. Drafted and submitted a comprehensive Departmental Review Petition to the Senior Secretary of the Ministry of Public Administration within thirty days, demonstrating the officer's unblemished Annual Confidential Report (ACR) record and proving that the procurement objection was grounded in statutory financial rules.
  2. When the ministry remained silent for two months, treated the appeal as constructively exhausted under Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980 and filed an Administrative Tribunal Case before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka.
  3. Argued before the District Judge presiding over the Tribunal that retiring an officer prematurely under the guise of 'public interest' as a disguised punishment without an inquiry violates the landmark principles of natural justice and Supreme Court precedents.
  4. The Administrative Tribunal delivered judgment declaring the compulsory retirement order unlawful, quashing the notification, and directing the ministry to reinstate the officer with full retroactive seniority and back pay.
  5. When the ministry appealed to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, our advocates defended the decree, securing a complete dismissal of the government's appeal and prompt treasury disbursement of all arrears.

faqs.question: Can I file a case in the Administrative Tribunal without a departmental appeal?
faqs.answer: No. Under Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980, exhausting all available departmental appeals or reviews is a mandatory statutory prerequisite. Filing without exhausting internal appeals will result in threshold dismissal.

faqs.question: What is the time limit to file a case in the Administrative Tribunal?
faqs.answer: Under Section 4(2), the application must be filed within six (6) months from the date of the departmental appeal decision, or within six months after waiting two months for an undecided appeal.

faqs.question: Can an ordinary civil court hear a government employee service case?
faqs.answer: No. Under Article 117 of the Constitution and Section 4 of Act No. VII of 1981, Administrative Tribunals have exclusive jurisdiction. Ordinary Assistant Judge and Joint District Judge courts are statutorily barred.

faqs.question: Can the Administrative Tribunal reinstate a dismissed employee with back pay?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Administrative Tribunal possesses full judicial powers to set aside wrongful dismissals, quash disciplinary orders, and direct the government to reinstate the employee with retroactive seniority and full salary arrears.

faqs.question: Can the government withhold pension benefits for audit objections?
faqs.answer: Under established Supreme Court precedents, pension is a property right earned through service and cannot be withheld for unresolved audit objections unless a formal judicial conviction for financial defalcation exists.

faqs.question: Where do I appeal if the Administrative Tribunal rules against me?
faqs.answer: An appeal must be filed within three (3) months before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal (AAT) in Dhaka under Section 6 of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980.

faqs.question: Can a High Court Writ Petition be filed directly for service matters?
faqs.answer: Generally, no, because Article 117(2) bars writ jurisdiction where an Administrative Tribunal exists. Writs are admitted only in narrow instances challenging the constitutional validity of service laws or where the tribunal has no jurisdiction.

faqs.question: Can family members of a deceased government servant file a tribunal case?
faqs.answer: Yes. Legal heirs and dependent family members can file an application before the Administrative Tribunal to claim withheld family pensions, gratuities, GPF balances, and statutory death benefits.
